paragraphs.en: Is it {true} that our brain alone is {responsible} for human cognition ( (认知) )? What about our body? Is it possible for thought and behavior to {originate} from {somewhere} other than our brain? {Psychologists} who study Embodied Cognition (EC (，具身认知) ) ask similar questions.The EC {theory} suggests our body also plays a role in thinking or {problem-solving} .More {precisely} , the mind shapes the body, and the body shapes the mind in equal {measure} .
paragraphs.cn: 人类的认知仅仅是由我们的大脑 <u> 负责的 </u> ，这是 <u> 真的 </u> 吗？我们的身体呢？思想和行为有可能 <u> 源自 </u> 大脑之外的 <u> 其他 </u> <u> 地方 </u> 吗？研究具身认知的 <u> 心理学家 </u> 也提出过类似的问题。具身认知 <u> 理论 </u> 表明，我们的身体在思考或 <u> 解决问题 </u> 的过程中也发挥着作用。更 <u> 准确地 </u> 说，头脑塑造着身体，而身体也以同样的 <u> 方式 </u> 塑造着头脑。

paragraphs.en: If you think about it for a moment, it makes {total} sense.When you {smell} something good or hear {amusing} sounds, certain emotions are {awakened} .Think about how {newborns} use their senses to understand the world around them.They don't have emotions so much as they have needs—they don't feel {sad} , they're just {hungry} and need food.Even {unborn} {babies} can feel their mothers’ {heartbeats} and this has a calming effect.In the real world, they {cry} when they're cold and then get {hugged} .That way, they start to associate being warm with being loved.
paragraphs.cn: 如果你稍加思考，就会发现这 <u> 完全 </u> 说得通。当你 <u> 闻 </u> 到好闻的气味或听到 <u> 有趣的 </u> 声音时，某些情绪就会被 <u> 唤醒 </u> 。想想 <u> 新生儿 </u> 是如何利用他们的感官来了解周围世界的吧。他们几乎没有情感，只有需求——他们不会感到 <u> 悲伤 </u> ，只是 <u> 饿 </u> 了，需要食物。甚至 <u> 未出生的婴儿 </u> 也能感受到母亲的 <u> 心跳 </u> ，这具有抚慰作用。在现实世界中，他们冷的时候会 <u> 哭 </u> ，然后就会得到 <u> 拥抱 </u> 。这样一来，他们就开始将温暖和被爱联系起来。

paragraphs.en: {Understandably} , {theorists} have been {arguing} for years and still {disagree} on whether the brain is the {nerve} {center} that operates the rest of the body.Older {Western} philosophers and {mainstream} language researchers believe this is fact, while the EC theory {theorizes} that the brain and body work together as an {organic} {supercomputer} , processing everything and forming your reactions.
paragraphs.cn: <u> 可以理解的是 </u> ， <u> 理论家 </u> 们多年来一直在 <u> 争论 </u> ，而对于大脑是否是控制身体其他部分的 <u> 神经中枢 </u> 这一问题，至今仍然 <u> 意见不一 </u> 。 <u> 西方 </u> 老一辈哲学家和 <u> 主流的 </u> 语言研究者认为这是事实，而具身认知理论则 <u> 认为 </u> 大脑和身体像 <u> 有机超级计算机 </u> 一样协同工作，处理一切事情并形成你的反应。

paragraphs.en: Further studies have {backed} up the mind-body interaction.In one experiment, test subjects were asked to judge people after being handed a {hot} or a cold drink.They all made warm {evaluations} when their fingertips {perceived} {warmth} rather than {coolness} .And it works the other way too; in another study, subjects' fingertip {temperatures} were measured after being “included” in or “rejected” from a group task.Those who were included felt physically warmer.
paragraphs.cn: 进一步的研究 <u> 证实 </u> 了身心的相互作用。在一项实验中，实验对象被要求在拿到 <u> 热 </u> 饮或冷饮后对他人进行评价。当他们的指尖 <u> 感受 </u> 到 <u> 温暖 </u> 而非 <u> 冰冷 </u> 时，他们都做出了“温暖”的 <u> 评价 </u> 。反之亦然。在另一项研究中，研究对象在参与一项小组任务时被“接纳”或“排斥”后，被测量了指尖 <u> 温度 </u> 。那些被“接纳”的人感觉身体更温暖。

paragraphs.en: For further {proof} , we can look at the metaphors ( (暗喻) ) that we use without even thinking.A {sympathetic} person is {frequently referred} to as one with a soft heart and someone who is very strong and {firm} in difficult situations is often described as {solid} as a rock.And this kind of metaphorical ( (比喻性的) ) use is common {across} languages.
paragraphs.cn: 为了找到进一步的 <u> 证据 </u> ，我们可以看看我们甚至不假思索就会使用的暗喻。我们 <u> 常说 </u> 一个 <u> 富有同情心的 </u> 人“心肠很软”，而在困境中非常坚强、 <u> 坚定的 </u> 人常常被描述为“ <u> 坚 </u> 如磐石”。这种比喻性的用法在 <u> 各种 </u> 语言中都很常见。

paragraphs.en: Now that you have the knowledge of mind-body interaction, why not use it? If you're going through your {worst} day, a warm {cup} of tea will give you a flash of pleasure.If you know you're physically cold, warm up before making any {interpersonal} decisions.
paragraphs.cn: 既然你已经掌握了身心互动的知识，为什么不加以利用呢？如果你正在经历 <u> 最糟糕的 </u> 一天，一 <u> 杯 </u> 热茶会给你带来一丝愉悦。如果你觉得身体很冷，那么在做出任何 <u> 人际交往的 </u> 决定之前，先暖暖身子吧。 5NoOncib/NjiX02BpMIzP+Fxyt/ox+WDCb+dhfH7KaYaJ4u5RsVmLondVmcHiLum9J1BQErGzJvzqa5GEIz4ZA==
